gloss: serpent; copper, bronze; seek omens, divine
summary: Three groups of words share these letters. נָחָשׁ is the snake, the creature that goes on its belly and bites (Gen 3:14; Ecc 10:8): the serpent of Eden that Yahweh God had made and that deceived the woman (Gen 3:1, 13), the burning serpents of the wilderness, and the bronze serpent Moses lifted on a pole (Num 21:6–9), which Jesus took as the figure of his own lifting up (Jhn 3:14). נְחֹשֶׁת, with נְחוּשָׁה and Aramaic נְחָשׁ, is copper and its alloy bronze, dug from the hills (Deu 8:9): the metal of the altar, the laver and the temple’s pillars, of fetters (in the dual), and of hardness and strength. The verb נִחֵשׁ and the noun נַחַשׁ are seeking and reading omens (1Ki 20:33; Num 23:23), which the law forbids (Lev 19:26; Deu 18:10). Ugaritic nḥš “snake”, Arabic nuḥās and Phoenician nḥšt “copper”, and Aramaic נַחֵשׁ “divine” each match one group; how the three meanings are related is not known.

words.gloss: copper, bronze; a thing of bronze; (dual) bronze fetters
words.summary: The red metal dug from the hills and its alloy with tin, worked since Tubal-cain (Gen 4:22): given and weighed for the tabernacle, cast into the altar, laver and pillars, made into armour, vessels and the serpent of Num 21. Below gold and silver in worth (Isa 60:17), it stands for what is hard and unyielding (Jer 1:18; Deu 28:23), and in the dual נְחֻשְׁתַּיִם for the fetters a captive is bound with.

senses.definition: The metal itself: mined from the rock, smelted and worked, counted among the metals with gold, silver, iron, tin and lead, brought as an offering, taken as spoil and traded.

evidence.note: “A land whose stones are iron, וּמֵהֲרָרֶיהָ תַּחְצֹב נְחֹשֶׁת, and out of whose hills you will dig copper”: a metal mined as ore, so copper, not only an alloy.
Tubal-cain, “a forger of every cutting tool of נְחֹשֶׁת and iron”.
“The gold, the silver, the נְחֹשֶׁת, the iron, the tin and the lead”: the metals that must pass through fire.
The offering for the tabernacle: “gold, silver and נְחֹשֶׁת”.
The bronze of the offering weighed: seventy talents and 2,400 shekels.
At Jericho the silver, gold, and vessels of bronze and iron are holy to Yahweh.
David takes very much bronze from Hadadezer’s cities.
David prepares bronze “in abundance without weight” for the house.
Javan, Tubal and Meshech trade “vessels of נְחֹשֶׁת” with Tyre.
“Two vessels of fine burnished נְחֹשֶׁת, precious as gold.”
“Instead of הַנְּחֹשֶׁת I will bring gold, and instead of iron silver, and instead of wood נְחֹשֶׁת”: ranked below gold and above wood.
Israel has become dross: “all of them נְחֹשֶׁת and tin and iron and lead in the furnace”, the base metals left when silver is refined out.
“They are all stubborn rebels … נְחֹשֶׁת and iron, all of them corrupt”: base metal, beside Jer 6:29–30 “refuse silver”.

senses.definition: The metal as the material of a made thing: the altar, its grate and vessels, the laver, the clasps and sockets of the tabernacle, the temple’s pillars and sea, armour, cooking vessels, censers, and the serpent Moses made.

evidence.note: The altar: “and you shall overlay it with נְחֹשֶׁת”.
“A laver of נְחֹשֶׁת and its base of נְחֹשֶׁת, for washing.”
The laver made from the mirrors of the women who served at the door of the tent.
מִזְבַּח הַנְּחֹשֶׁת and its grate.
A sin offering boiled in a כְּלִי נְחֹשֶׁת: the vessel is scoured and rinsed, where an earthen one is broken.
The bronze censers of Korah’s company beaten into plates for the altar.
“Moses made נְחַשׁ נְחֹשֶׁת”, a serpent of bronze.
Goliath’s helmet of נְחֹשֶׁת and coat weighing 5,000 shekels of נְחֹשֶׁת.
Hiram, a worker in נְחֹשֶׁת, filled with wisdom to do all work in it.
Ahaz moves “the altar of הַנְּחֹשֶׁת which was before Yahweh”.
The Chaldeans break up the pillars, the stands and the sea, and carry the bronze to Babylon.
Cymbals of נְחֹשֶׁת for the singers.

senses.definition: The look of polished bronze, in visions of the cherubim and of a heavenly messenger: burnished, shining.

evidence.note: The living creatures’ feet “sparkled כְּעֵין נְחֹשֶׁת קָלָל”, like the gleam of burnished bronze.
The man in linen: “his arms and his feet כְּעֵין נְחֹשֶׁת קָלָל”.
“A man whose appearance was like the appearance of נְחֹשֶׁת”, with a measuring reed.
Four chariots come out from between two mountains, “and the mountains were mountains of נְחֹשֶׁת”.
The Son of man’s feet “like χαλκολίβανον, as if refined in a furnace”, taking up Dan 10:6.

senses.gloss: bronze (as a figure of hardness and strength)
senses.definition: Bronze as what does not give: walls no one breaks through, a sky that yields no rain, doors and shoes that hold.

evidence.note: “I have made you today a fortified city, an iron pillar, and חֹמוֹת נְחֹשֶׁת against the whole land”: the prophet will not be overcome.
“A fortified wall of נְחֹשֶׁת; they will fight against you, but they will not prevail.”
“Your heavens over your head will be נְחֹשֶׁת and the earth under you iron”: a sky shut against rain.
To Asher: “iron and נְחֹשֶׁת your bolts (or shoes), and as your days so your strength”.
“He has broken the doors of נְחֹשֶׁת and cut the bars of iron.”
“Can one break iron, iron from the north, and נְחֹשֶׁת?”

senses.definition: In the dual נְחֻשְׁתַּיִם, a pair of bronze fetters for the feet or hands; once in the singular with a suffix, “my chain”.

evidence.note: The Philistines put out Samson’s eyes “and bound him בַּנְחֻשְׁתַּיִם”, and he ground in the prison.
David over Abner: “your hands were not bound, and your feet were not put לִנְחֻשְׁתַּיִם”.
Zedekiah blinded “and bound בַּנְחֻשְׁתַּיִם” and brought to Babylon.
Manasseh taken with hooks, bound בַּנְחֻשְׁתַּיִם, and carried to Babylon.
“He has walled me in and I cannot go out; הִכְבִּיד נְחָשְׁתִּי, he has made my chain heavy.”

senses.definition: Once, of Jerusalem pictured as an adulterous wife: “because נְחֻשְׁתֵּךְ was poured out and your nakedness uncovered in your harlotries”. The verses before say she paid her lovers instead of being paid (Ezk 16:33–34), which fits “your copper”, money, poured out on them; but the word is not used of money elsewhere, and the parallel with nakedness leaves it uncertain.

evidence.note: יַעַן הִשָּׁפֵךְ נְחֻשְׁתֵּךְ וַתִּגָּלֶה עֶרְוָתֵךְ בְּתַזְנוּתַיִךְ.
“You gave your gifts to all your lovers and bribed them … you give hire, and no hire is given to you.”

greek.gloss: copper, bronze; a thing of bronze

evidence.locator: נְחֹשֶׁת → χαλκός ×59 (lemma count, MACULA alignment); Exo.27.2, נְחֹשֶׁת → χαλκῷ; Lam.3.7, נְחָשְׁתִּי → χαλκόν

evidence.note: Babylon’s cargo includes vessels “of χαλκοῦ and iron and marble”.
“No χαλκόν in their belt”: copper coin.
“Sounding χαλκός”, a bronze gong.

evidence.locator: נְחֹשֶׁת → χάλκεος ×52; Num.21.9, נְחַשׁ נְחֹשֶׁת → ὄφιν χαλκοῦν

evidence.note: Idols “of gold and silver and χαλκᾶ and stone and wood”, which neither see nor hear, as in Dan 5:23.
The man of the tombs had often been bound with πέδαις and chains.

parallels.note: Iron is its constant partner: tools, the hard sky and earth, doors and bars, bolts.
Gold, silver and bronze are the offering’s three metals, bronze the least of them; Isaiah promises gold in its place.

phrases.gloss: walls of bronze (of a prophet made unassailable)

words.summary: The snake: it goes on its belly, bites, carries venom, can be charmed, and lies in walls and on rocks. It is the serpent of Eden, one of the living things Yahweh God made, which deceived the woman and was cursed to eat dust; the burning serpents of the wilderness and the bronze one made in their likeness; Leviathan, the fleeing serpent Yahweh slays; and a figure of men whose tongues are venom.

senses.definition: A living creature that moves on its belly, eats dust, lies on rocks and in walls, and bites with venom; a bite may kill, and some can be charmed.

evidence.note: “On your belly you shall go, and dust you shall eat all the days of your life.”
“Whoever breaks through a wall, a נָחָשׁ will bite him.”
“If the נָחָשׁ bites before it is charmed (בְּלוֹא־לָחַשׁ), the charmer has no advantage.”
“Their venom is like the venom of a נָחָשׁ, like a deaf adder (פֶּתֶן) that stops its ear”, which will not hear the charmers (58:6).
“I am sending נְחָשִׁים among you, adders that cannot be charmed, and they will bite you.”
“The way of a נָחָשׁ on a rock”, one of the four things too wonderful to know.
A man escapes the lion and the bear, leans his hand on the wall of his house, “and the נָחָשׁ bites him”.
Even at the bottom of the sea “I will command the נָחָשׁ and it will bite them”.
The great and terrible wilderness, “נָחָשׁ שָׂרָף and scorpion”.
Yahweh sent “הַנְּחָשִׁים הַשְּׂרָפִים”, the burning serpents; they bit the people and many died.
“Pray to Yahweh that he take away the נָחָשׁ from us.”
Moses’ staff, thrown down, became a נָחָשׁ, and he fled from it.
“The staff that was turned into a נָחָשׁ”: the sign of 7:9–10 calls it a תַּנִּין.
Wine “at the last bites like a נָחָשׁ and stings like an adder”.
In Yahweh’s holy mountain the wolf and lamb feed together, “and dust shall be the serpent’s food”.
The nations “shall lick the dust like the נָחָשׁ”.

senses.definition: The serpent of the garden: one of the living things of the field that Yahweh God had made, more cunning than them all, which spoke to the woman, contradicted God’s word, deceived her, and was cursed above every beast.

evidence.note: “And הַנָּחָשׁ was more cunning (עָרוּם) than any living thing of the field which Yahweh God had made”: a creature, among the beasts.
“You will not surely die”, against God’s “you will surely die” (Gen 2:17).
The woman: “הַנָּחָשׁ deceived me, and I ate.”
Cursed “above all the livestock and above every living thing of the field”.
“As the ὄφις deceived Eve by its craftiness.”
“Adam was not deceived, but the woman, being deceived, fell into transgression.”
“The great dragon, the old ὄφις, called the false accuser and the adversary, who deceives the whole world.”

senses.definition: The serpent of bronze that Moses made at Yahweh’s word and set on a pole, so that anyone bitten who looked at it lived; later burned incense to, and broken by Hezekiah.

evidence.note: “Moses made נְחַשׁ נְחֹשֶׁת and set it on the pole, and if a נָחָשׁ had bitten a man, he looked to נְחַשׁ הַנְּחֹשֶׁת and lived.”
Yahweh’s command calls it a שָׂרָף, a burning one, the name of the serpents that bit them (21:6).
Hezekiah “broke in pieces נְחַשׁ הַנְּחֹשֶׁת that Moses had made, for until those days the children of Israel burned incense to it”.
“As Moses lifted up the ὄφιν in the wilderness, so must the Son of man be lifted up.”

senses.definition: In poetry, the fleeing, twisting serpent, Leviathan, set with the תַּנִּין of the sea, which Yahweh pierces or punishes with his sword: a figure of a power that opposes him.

evidence.note: “In that day Yahweh will punish with his sword … Leviathan נָחָשׁ בָּרִחַ, and Leviathan נָחָשׁ עֲקַלָּתוֹן, and he will slay the תַּנִּין that is in the sea.”
“By his breath the heavens are fair; his hand has pierced נָחָשׁ בָּרִיחַ”, beside Rahab whom he smote (26:12).
Yahweh’s arm “that cut Rahab, that pierced the תַּנִּין”, of the crossing of the sea; Isa 30:7 names Egypt Rahab.

senses.definition: A person, tribe or nation likened to a serpent: one that bites from ambush, or whose tongue carries venom, or whose voice is the hiss of a serpent going away.

evidence.note: “Dan shall be a נָחָשׁ by the way, a horned snake (שְׁפִיפֹן) by the path, that bites the horse’s heels.”
“They sharpen their tongue like a נָחָשׁ; adder’s venom is under their lips.”
Egypt: “her voice goes like a נָחָשׁ” as the woodcutters come against her.
To Philistia: “from the root of the נָחָשׁ shall come an adder, and its fruit a flying burning one”.
“ὄφεις, offspring of vipers.”

evidence.locator: נָחָשׁ → ὄφις ×26 (lemma count, MACULA alignment); Gen.3.1, הַנָּחָשׁ → ὄφις; Num.21.9, נְחַשׁ → ὄφιν; Isa.27.1

evidence.note: The bronze serpent of Num 21:9.
“Nor let us tempt Christ as some of them tempted, and were destroyed by τῶν ὄφεων”: Num 21:6.
The serpent of Gen 3.
“Wise as ὄφεις”, as the serpent was cunning (Gen 3:1).
“Authority to tread on ὄφεων and scorpions”, the pair of Deu 8:15.

evidence.locator: נָחָשׁ → δράκων ×2: Job.26.13, נָחָשׁ בָּרִיחַ → δράκοντα; Amo.9.3, הַנָּחָשׁ → δράκοντι

evidence.note: “The great δράκων, the old ὄφις”: the two renderings of נָחָשׁ together.

parallels.note: Adder or viper, set beside it for biting and venom.
A horned snake lying by the path.
An adder or viper, whose venom is under the lips.
“Burning one”: the wilderness serpents, and the bronze one made in their likeness.
The staff became a תַּנִּין before Pharaoh and is then called a נָחָשׁ; Isaiah sets the sea’s תַּנִּין beside Leviathan the serpent.
Serpent and scorpion, the dangers of the wilderness.

phrases.gloss: lick the dust like the serpent (be humbled)

words.summary: Only in the piel: to look for and read omens, signs taken from chance events or from an object such as a cup, to learn what is hidden or what is coming. The law forbids it among the practices of the nations. How it is related to the root’s “serpent” and “copper” is not known.

stems.gloss: seek omens, practise divination; learn by an omen

senses.definition: To watch for a sign in what happens or is said, and take it as revealing what is hidden or what will be; to come to know something by such a sign.

evidence.note: Ben-hadad’s men “וְהָאֲנָשִׁים יְנַחֲשׁוּ”, were watching for an omen, and quickly seized on Ahab’s word: “Your brother Ben-hadad!”: a chance word taken as a sign.
Laban: “נִחַשְׁתִּי, I have learned by omen, that Yahweh has blessed me for your sake.”
Joseph’s cup: “is it not the one my lord drinks from, וְהוּא נַחֵשׁ יְנַחֵשׁ בּוֹ, and he indeed divines by it?”
“Did you not know that such a man as I can indeed divine?”: part of Joseph’s testing of his brothers; Joseph had told Pharaoh’s servants that interpretations belong to God (Gen 40:8).
“You shall not eat with the blood; לֹא תְנַחֲשׁוּ, and you shall not practise soothsaying (תְעוֹנֵנוּ).”
“There shall not be found among you … one who uses divinations (קֹסֵם קְסָמִים), a soothsayer, וּמְנַחֵשׁ, or a sorcerer.”
Israel “used divinations וַיְנַחֵשׁוּ, and sold themselves to do evil”.
Manasseh “practised soothsaying וְנִחֵשׁ, and dealt with mediums”.

parallels.note: Divine, use divinations: listed with it among the practices of the nations.

words.summary: A poetic form of נְחֹשֶׁת, all in verse: the metal smelted from stone, the bronze bow and doors, and above all bronze as the figure of what is hard and strong.

senses.gloss: copper, bronze (the metal, and things of it)
senses.definition: The metal smelted out of stone, and a bow or doors made of it.

evidence.note: “Iron is taken from the dust, and stone is poured out as נְחוּשָׁה”: copper smelted from ore.
“My arms bend a bow of נְחוּשָׁה.”
He flees the iron weapon, and a bow of נְחוּשָׁה pierces him.
To Cyrus: “I will break the doors of נְחוּשָׁה and cut the bars of iron.”

senses.gloss: bronze (as a figure of hardness and strength)
senses.definition: Bronze as what will not give: a land that yields nothing, an unbending forehead, hooves that crush, bones that do not break.

evidence.note: “I will make your heavens like iron and your land כַּנְּחֻשָׁה”: hard, yielding no crop.
“You are obstinate; your neck is an iron sinew and your forehead נְחוּשָׁה.”
“Arise and thresh, daughter of Zion, for I will make your horn iron and your hooves נְחוּשָׁה, and you will beat in pieces many peoples.”
Behemoth: “his bones are tubes of נְחוּשָׁה, his limbs like bars of iron”.
Leviathan “counts iron as straw, נְחוּשָׁה as rotten wood”.

words.summary: The Aramaic of Daniel for bronze: the belly and thighs of Nebuchadnezzar’s image, the third kingdom, the band on the stump, the gods of bronze, and the fourth beast’s claws.

senses.definition: The metal, ranked with gold, silver, iron and clay in the image, and among the materials of idols and of a binding band.

evidence.note: The image: head of fine gold, chest and arms of silver, “its belly and thighs דִּי נְחָשׁ”.
“A third kingdom, of נְחָשָׁא, which shall rule over all the earth.”
Iron, clay, נְחָשָׁא, silver and gold broken together and blown away; the stone becomes a great mountain.
The stump of the tree left “with a band of iron and נְחָשׁ”.
They praised the gods of gold and silver, נְחָשָׁא, iron, wood and stone.
Gods of bronze “which do not see or hear or know”; Rev 9:20 echoes it.
The fourth beast, “its teeth of iron and its claws דִּי־נְחָשׁ”.
Idols of gold, silver, bronze, stone and wood, which cannot see or hear, from Dan 5:23 (adjective χάλκεος).

words.summary: The omen sought by the verb’s practice, twice in Balaam’s story. BDB files Jer 8:17 נְחָשִׁים here as well, but there the word is plainly “serpents” that bite; it is counted under נָחָשׁ.

senses.definition: A sign sought and read to learn or to work an outcome; Balaam’s means of seeking a curse.

evidence.note: “For there is no נַחַשׁ in (or against) Jacob, and no קֶסֶם in Israel; now it shall be said of Jacob and Israel, What has God done!”
Balaam saw that it pleased Yahweh to bless Israel, “and did not go, as at other times, to meet נְחָשִׁים”.

parallels.note: Divination: the parallel term in Balaam’s oracle.

words.summary: Once, in Job’s complaint: made of bronze, and so able to bear anything.

senses.definition: Of bronze, as a figure of what can endure without breaking.

evidence.note: “Is my strength the strength of stones, or is my flesh נָחוּשׁ?”: Job is not able to endure endlessly.

words.summary: The name by which the bronze serpent was called when Hezekiah broke it: נְחֹשֶׁת with the ending ‑ān, “the bronze one”, sounding like נָחָשׁ “serpent” too. Whether the name was Israel’s for their idol or the scornful “a piece of bronze” of the one who broke it, the verse does not settle.

senses.gloss: Nehushtan, the bronze serpent so called
senses.definition: The bronze serpent Moses made, as it was called when it had become an object of incense-burning in Judah.

evidence.note: “He broke in pieces the bronze serpent that Moses had made, for until those days the children of Israel burned incense to it, וַיִּקְרָא־לוֹ נְחֻשְׁתָּן.”

cognates.note: In an incantation against snakebite, mnt ntk nḥš “incantation for the bite of a snake”, with šmrr nḥš “the venom of the snake” (KTU 1.100:4–5, 58–59): the same creature that bites, with venom, and is countered by charming, as Ecc 10:11 and Psa 58:5–6. Segert’s glossary sorts it between nḥlt and nḥt, so with ḥ (not ḫ); Ugaritic keeps š and ṯ apart, and has š.

evidence.locator: p. 155, §86.73, an incantation against snake bite (KTU 1.100:1–7, 57–76)

cognates.gloss: a creature hunted or caught, including serpents and reptiles; (of a serpent) bite
cognates.note: Lane’s sources give ḥanaš as anything hunted of birds and of venomous creeping things such as serpents, and ḥanašathu al-ḥayya “the serpent bit him”; maḥnūš “bitten by a ḥanaš”. The meaning fits, but the first two letters stand in the other order and the Arabic ش normally answers to Hebrew שׂ, not ש; recorded as possible only.

“Copper: and brass … a species of ṣufr intensely red: a chaste Arabic word”; also fire, and the sparks that fly from brass or iron when it is beaten; naḥḥās a coppersmith. Arabic ḥ (ح) and s (س), the regular answer to Hebrew ש (š).

cognates.gloss: ill-omened, unlucky; ill omen, misfortune (of stars and days)
cognates.note: The verb is “was unprosperous, inauspicious, or unlucky”, said of a man and of a star; the noun is the contrary of saʿd “good fortune”, of stars and other things; yawm naḥs “an unlucky day”. It is the same consonants as נחש and belongs to reading fortune from signs, but it names the ill omen itself, not the seeking of omens; recorded as possible.

Phoenician and Punic inscriptions: “this altar of bronze” for the Lady of Byblos (KAI 10), a bowl “of the finest bronze” to Baal of Lebanon (KAI 31), a bronze plaque inscribed and nailed to a wall (KAI 43), a bronze altar to Eshmun (KAI 66). An Amarna letter from Byblos glosses it nuḫuštu (EA 69:28). The same word, feminine in -t, as נְחֹשֶׁת.

Jewish Aramaic, in the Targums for Hebrew נְחֹשֶׁת (Targ. Jer 15:20; Onkelos Num 21:9) and in the Talmud of copper money (“copper rises and falls”, silver being the standard); the denominative aphel אַנְחֵשׁ “use copper, plate”. Aramaic ח does not show whether ḥ or ḫ stands behind it.

evidence.note: Targ. Jer. XV, 20; Targ. Num. XXI, 9; Y. Kidd. I, 58ᵈ.

cognates.note: Jewish Aramaic: the pael in the Targum for Hebrew וְנִחֵשׁ (Targ. 2Ki 21:6; 17:17), and in the Talmud of one who “made his movements dependent on an omen”; the noun נַחֲשָׁא, pl. נַחְשִׁין, an omen (Targ. Y. II Num 23:23). The same sense of seeking and reading signs.

evidence.note: Pa. נַחֵישׁ; Targ. II Kings XXI, 6; XVII, 17; Ḥull. 95ᵇ.
Targ. Y. II, Num. XXIII, 23.

doctrine.statement: Genesis calls the נָחָשׁ one of “the living things of the field which Yahweh God had made”, more cunning than them all (Gen 3:1), and its sentence is an animal’s: cursed above all livestock, to go on its belly and eat dust (Gen 3:14). It contradicted God’s word, “you will surely die” (Gen 2:17), with “you will not surely die” (Gen 3:4), and the woman said, “the serpent deceived me” (Gen 3:13), as Paul repeats (2Co 11:3; 1Ti 2:14). God set enmity between its seed and the woman’s seed, who would bruise its head while it bruised his heel (Gen 3:15). Sin entered by one man, and death by sin (Rom 5:12); the sting of death is sin (1Co 15:56). Revelation calls the power that deceives the world “the old serpent, called the false accuser and the adversary” (Rev 12:9; 20:2), and Hebrews says the Son shared flesh and blood “that through death he might destroy the one having the power of death, that is, the false accuser” (Heb 2:14). From the verses: the serpent of Eden was a creature God made, and nothing in Genesis makes it more; what it brought was a lie that, believed and acted on, brought sin and death. Scripture then uses “the old serpent” for that lie and for sin’s power over men, and the woman’s seed destroys it in his own death.

When the people spoke against God, Yahweh sent the burning serpents and many died; when they confessed “we have sinned”, he had Moses make a serpent of bronze and set it on a pole, and whoever was bitten and looked to it lived (Num 21:5–9). Paul warns, “nor let us tempt Christ, as some of them tempted and were destroyed by the serpents” (1Co 10:9). Jesus says, “as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of man be lifted up, that whoever believes in him should not perish but have eternal life” (Jhn 3:14–15), and “lifted up” signified the death he would die (Jhn 12:32–33). God sent his own Son “in the likeness of sinful flesh, and for sin, condemned sin in the flesh” (Rom 8:3), and made him who knew no sin to be sin for us (2Co 5:21), tempted in all points as we are, yet without sin (Heb 4:15). From the verses: what was lifted up had the form of the thing that was killing them, yet no venom of its own; so Christ bore the nature in which sin works, without sinning, and in his being lifted up on the cross sin was condemned; life comes by looking to him in faith. The bronze serpent itself was afterwards burned incense to, and Hezekiah broke it in pieces as a mere “Nehushtan” (2Ki 18:4): the sign given for healing was never to be worshipped.

The law forbids נִחֵשׁ beside eating with the blood and soothsaying (Lev 19:26), and lists the מְנַחֵשׁ among the practices of the nations Israel was dispossessing, for which Yahweh would give instead a prophet like Moses with his words in his mouth (Deu 18:10–18); Peter says that prophet is Jesus (Act 3:22–23). Balaam, hired to curse, says “there is no נַחַשׁ in Jacob, no קֶסֶם in Israel”, and when he sees that Yahweh wills to bless Israel he stops going to meet omens (Num 23:23; 24:1). Israel’s and Manasseh’s omen-seeking are counted among the evils that provoked Yahweh and brought their ruin (2Ki 17:17; 21:6; 2Ch 33:6). From the verses: Yahweh’s people are to learn what is hidden and what is coming from his word through his prophet, not from omens; and no omen avails against those he has blessed.

In Nebuchadnezzar’s image the belly and thighs are נְחָשׁ, “a third kingdom of bronze, which shall rule over all the earth” (Dan 2:32, 39), after Babylon’s gold and the silver kingdom that follows it; Daniel 8 names the kingdoms that follow Babylon as Media-Persia and then Greece (Dan 8:20–21). The stone cut out without hands strikes the image on its feet, and then the iron, clay, bronze, silver and gold are broken in pieces together and blown away, while the stone becomes a mountain filling the earth (Dan 2:34–35, 45): “the God of heaven will set up a kingdom which shall never be destroyed … it shall break in pieces and consume all these kingdoms, and it shall stand for ever” (Dan 2:44). From the verses: the bronze kingdom is Greece, and though it passed long before the feet, the image stands as one until the stone strikes; the kingdoms of men are ended together when God sets up his own kingdom on the earth.

note: Drafted 2026-11-13. BDB keys: n.cw.ab (נְחֹשֶׁת “copper”) and n.cx.ab (נְחֹשֶׁת “lust, harlotry”) list the same 140 tokens; the entry names n.cw.ab only and keeps Ezk 16:36 as a sense of that word (“ezk-16-36”), with its meaning left open. n.cu.ab (serpent, 42 tokens) shares its tokens of the name Nahash with n.cu.ac, so its count includes them. BDB files Jer 8:17 נְחָשִׁים under the noun נַחַשׁ (n.cv.ab) too; it is entered under נָחָשׁ. Left out as names: נָחָשׁ Nahash (n.cu.ac: the Ammonite king(s), the father of Abigail), נְחֻשְׁתָּא Nehushta (n.cw.ae, Jehoiachin’s mother), and the place עִיר נָחָשׁ Ir-nahash (p.cm.ag, 0 tokens); נַחְשׁוֹן Nahshon has its own name entry (names/nahshon.json). נְחֻשְׁתָּן Nehushtan is kept as a word, since it names the bronze serpent, not a person, though TIPNR keeps a Supernatural record for it (Nehushtan@2Ki.18.4). Open questions: (1) whether “serpent”, “copper” and “seek omens” are one older root: the cognates show ḥ and š for both serpent (Ugaritic) and copper (Arabic), so no merged-letter split is visible; no verse or cognate ties them, and the summary says so. (2) Arabic naḥs “ill omen” is recorded as possible for the divination words; with only the Jewish Aramaic pael as a sure cognate, the omen words rest mostly on their own verses. (3) Ezk 16:36 נְחֻשְׁתֵּךְ: “your money” from context (16:33–34) is offered as likely, not settled. Leads not followed: Syriac ܢܚܫܐ “copper” and ܢܚܫܐ “augury” (Wiktionary leads; Payne Smith not checked; the Peshitta New Testament has no word of this root in SEDRA); Ge’ez ናሐስ naḥās “copper” (Wiktionary; Dillmann and Leslau not checked); no Akkadian cognate found (Akkadian nēšu “lion”, offered for a Proto-Semitic *naḥaš, is not followed). The verb’s and noun נַחַשׁ’s Septuagint rendering is οἰωνίζομαι / οἰωνισμός, which the New Testament does not use, so no Greek is recorded for them.
